461.quote_or_event: “Three merchants set out on their travels, each with his capital; one of them gained there much, the second returned with his capital, and the third merchant came home after having lost his capital. This parable is taken from common life; learn (to apply it) to the Law.”
461.explanation: Mahavira's sermon uses a merchant's ledger of capital, gain and loss to teach how a human life should be spent, and closes by saying the wise man weighs the outcomes in his mind before choosing his course (7.30).
461.tie_back: The Kural's three-part reckoning of what is spent, what is gained and the net profit matches the parable's capital, profit and loss almost term for term.
461.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.14–15 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
461._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. The ledger vocabulary matches closely; the Jain text applies it to spiritual rather than worldly undertakings.

462.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sūtras.”
462.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's path to deliverance begins with choosing one's company: serve the teachers, shun fools, study, and reflect. The next verses tell the monk to select a companion of right understanding who equals or surpasses him in virtue (32.4–5).
462.tie_back: Like the Kural, it joins careful choice of counsellors with one's own examination and reflection as the way to reach what is otherwise hard to attain.
462.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.3 (cf. 32.4–5) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
462._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Strong fit on chosen associates plus personal reflection; the Jain goal is liberation, not success in worldly undertakings.

463.quote_or_event: “As a man for the sake of one Kâkinî (risks and) loses a thousand (Kârshâpaṇas), or as the king lost his kingdom (and life) by eating a mango-fruit which he was strictly forbidden (by his physician)”
463.explanation: Two short examples show the folly of staking something great for a trifling gain: a thousand coins thrown away for a copper, a kingdom lost for one forbidden mango.
463.tie_back: The Kural warns the wise not to put their capital at risk for a hoped-for gain, and the Jain verse pictures exactly that bad bargain.
463.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
463._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close match on risking principal for small gain; in context the verse compares human pleasures with heavenly ones.

464.quote_or_event: “Dirgha-darsi : Far-sighted.” … “Salajja : Actuated by a sense of shame.”
464.explanation: Hemacandra's list of the qualities of an ideal Jain layman includes being far-sighted and being moved by a sense of shame, alongside not engaging in a reprehensible occupation.
464.tie_back: The Kural's prudent man avoids unclear ventures because he fears disgrace; Hemacandra's householder combines the same foresight with a lively sense of shame.
464.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
464._accuracy_note: The two items are quoted verbatim from Sangave's English rendering on jainworld.com, a secondary source. These are separate list entries that I have put together, not a single teaching on doubtful undertakings.

465.quote_or_event: “Making Faith his fortress, Penance and Self-control the bolt (of its gate), Patience its strong wall, so that guarded in three ways it is impregnable; making Zeal his bow, its string Carefulness in walking (iriyâ), and its top (where the string is fastened) Content, he should bend (this bow) with Truth, piercing with the arrow, Penance, (the foe's) mail, Karman--(in this way) a sage will be the victor in battle and get rid of the Saṃsâra.”
465.explanation: When Indra urges King Nami to fortify his city, Nami answers that the real campaign is fought against karma, and he lists in detail the fortress, wall, bow, string and arrow it requires.
465.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning against attacking a foe without thorough planning, Nami's war against karma is to be fought only once every defence and weapon has been prepared.
465.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.20–22 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
465._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Jainism rejects outward warfare, so this inner campaign matches only the Kural's point about thorough preparation, not its military advice.

466.quote_or_event: “One should desist from one thing, and practise another: desist from neglect of self-control, and practise self-control.”
466.explanation: The lecture on the monk's mode of life opens with a double rule: some things must be given up and others actively practised.
466.tie_back: The Kural says ruin comes both from doing what should not be done and from failing to do what should; the Jain verse likewise demands both abstaining and acting.
466.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 31.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
466._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Same two-sided structure of omission and commission; the Jain verse does not stress ruin as the result.

467.quote_or_event: “Vratas or a vow is a solemn resolve made after deliberation to observe a particular rule of conduct … A vow affords stability to the will and guards its votary from the evils of temptation or of unguarded life”
467.explanation: Jain ethics defines the vow, the basic unit of a layman's discipline, as a resolve taken only after deliberation, which then keeps the will steady.
467.tie_back: The Kural's order (reflect, then resolve, and do not reopen the question afterwards) is how the Jain vow works: deliberation comes first, and steadiness follows.
467.source: Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code', section on the twelve vratas (jainworld.com)
467._accuracy_note: Quoted verbatim from Sangave's modern secondary account on jainworld.com, not from a scriptural verse. It is a strong conceptual match.

468.quote_or_event: “If an ignorant man should eat but a blade of Kuśa-grass every month, (the merit of his penance) will not equal the sixteenth part of his who possesses the Law as it has been taught.”
468.explanation: Nami tells Indra that even the harshest austerity, done without right knowledge, is worth almost nothing next to practice guided by the true teaching.
468.tie_back: The Kural says effort spent without the proper method will fail however much it is supported; Jainism likewise holds that great toil without the right way yields little.
468.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 9.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
468._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close in logic (effort without right method is wasted), though the Kural's image of many supporters is absent.

469.quote_or_event: “The effect of giving of the gift–dāna–has distinctions based on the specific manner in which it is given–vidhiviśeṣa, the specific thing given–dravyaviśeṣa, the specific nature of the giver–dātṛviśeṣa, and the specific nature of the recipient–pātraviśeṣa.”
469.explanation: Umasvati teaches that the fruit of a gift depends on how it is given, what is given, who gives and who receives. Pujyapada's commentary compares this to seed whose harvest depends on the soil.
469.tie_back: The Kural warns that even doing good can fail if one ignores each person's nature, and the Jain sutra makes the recipient's nature one of the factors that decide a gift's result.
469.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.39, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
469._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib.org. Good fit on suiting a benefit to its recipient; the Jain concern is merit, not political hostility.

470.quote_or_event: “Prasiddham desacharam samacharan : Following the reputable usages of the country.” … “Adsa-kalayoh charyam tyajan : Avoiding action which is inappropriate to time and place.”
470.explanation: Among the qualities Hemacandra expects of a Jain householder are keeping to the respected customs of the land and avoiding conduct out of keeping with time and place.
470.tie_back: The Kural's final test is that an act should be fitting so the world does not scorn it, and Hemacandra's layman measures his conduct by the same standard of social fitness.
470.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
470._accuracy_note: Both items are quoted verbatim from Sangave's English rendering on jainworld.com (a secondary source, spelling as printed). They are reasonable but partial, since the Kural's point about fitting one's own station is not explicit.
